modules.title: 1 · Unit roots and spurious regression
modules.summary: Distinguish persistent stochastic trends from stable relationships.

stages.title: Unit roots and spurious regression: research guide
stages.html:
Unit roots and spurious regression

Distinguish persistent stochastic trends from stable relationships.

Unrelated integrated series can produce impressive t statistics and R-squared; residual persistence reveals the spurious fit.

Workflow. Specify deterministic terms and interpret tests with their low-power limitations.

Diagnostic: Inspect trend specification, lag length, and complementary evidence. The main failure to avoid is classifying persistence from one test statistic alone.

stages.title: Unit-root testing intuition lab
stages.note: Regress one series on a totally unrelated one — push persistence toward 1 and watch the spurious t-stat and R-squared explode even though nothing links them.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); phi = {{phi}}
def ar1(phi, n, rng):
    e = rng.normal(0, 1, n); y = np.zeros(n)
    for t in range(1, n):
        y[t] = phi*y[t-1] + e[t]
    return y
x = ar1(phi, n, rng)      # two INDEPENDENT series
y = ar1(phi, n, rng)      # nothing links them at all
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
tstat = res.tvalues[1]; r2 = res.rsquared
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
ax[0].plot(x, color='#da9100', lw=1.2, label='x')
ax[0].plot(y, color='#4f8fba', lw=1.2, label='y')
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8); ax[0].set_title('Two INDEPENDENT series')
ax[1].scatter(x, y, s=10, color='#8888aa', alpha=0.5)
xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 50)
ax[1].plot(xs, res.params[0] + res.params[1]*xs, color='#c0392b', lw=2)
ax[1].set_title(f'|t|={abs(tstat):.1f}   R2={r2:.2f}')
plt.tight_layout()
print(f'phi={phi:.2f}  n={n}  slope t-stat={tstat:.2f}  R2={r2:.3f}')
print('These series are unrelated, so an honest |t| should exceed 2 only ~5% of the time.')

modules.title: 2 · Engle-Granger cointegration
modules.summary: Test whether a linear combination of integrated variables is stationary.

stages.title: Engle-Granger cointegration: research guide
stages.html:
Engle-Granger cointegration

Test whether a linear combination of integrated variables is stationary.

Residual-based critical values differ from ordinary unit-root tests because the long-run relation is estimated first.

Workflow. Estimate a long-run relation and test whether its residual is stationary with correct critical values.

Diagnostic: Inspect residual-based unit-root evidence and normalization. The main failure to avoid is using ordinary unit-root critical values on estimated residuals.

stages.title: Engle-Granger cointegration intuition lab
stages.note: Two series share a stochastic trend; slide the equilibrium-error persistence toward 1 and watch the residual stop mean-reverting and the residual-based cointegration p-value collapse.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint, adfuller
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200; rho = {{rho}}; beta = {{beta}}
trend = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, n))        # common I(1) stochastic trend
z = np.zeros(n)                               # equilibrium error, AR(1) rho
for t in range(1, n):
    z[t] = rho*z[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 0.5)
x = trend + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)
y = beta*trend + z                            # y and x share the trend
t_eg, p_eg, _ = coint(y, x)                   # residual-based critical values
res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()     # step 1: long-run relation
resid = res.resid                             # step 2: test this residual
adf_p = adfuller(resid, autolag='AIC')[1]     # WRONG crit values for est. resid
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
ax[0].plot(x, color='#da9100', label='x'); ax[0].plot(y, color='#4f8fba', label='y')
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8); ax[0].set_title('Levels share a trend')
ax[1].plot(resid, color='#c0392b'); ax[1].axhline(0, color='#888', lw=0.8)
ax[1].set_title('Estimated equilibrium residual')
plt.tight_layout()
print(f'rho={rho:.2f}  beta_hat={res.params[1]:.2f} (true {beta:.2f})')
print(f'Engle-Granger p={p_eg:.3f} (residual-based crit) vs naive ADF-on-residual p={adf_p:.3f}')

modules.title: 3 · Johansen systems and rank
modules.summary: Determine how many stationary long-run relations a multivariate system contains.

stages.title: Johansen systems and rank: research guide
stages.html:
Johansen systems and rank

Determine how many stationary long-run relations a multivariate system contains.

Rank tests depend on deterministic terms and lag order; normalization then gives interpretable cointegrating vectors.

Workflow. Determine cointegration rank in a system before interpreting vectors.

Diagnostic: Inspect deterministic specification, lag order, trace and maximum-eigenvalue tests. The main failure to avoid is selecting a rank without matching the system specification.

stages.title: Johansen rank analysis intuition lab
stages.note: A 3-variable system truly has rank 1; raise measurement noise or change the lag order and watch the trace test miscount the stationary long-run relations.
stages.template:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.vector_ar.vecm import coint_johansen
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 300; sig = {{sigma}}; klag = int({{klag}})
alpha = np.array([-0.4, 0.4, 0.0])          # error-correction loadings
beta = np.array([1.0, -1.0, 0.0])           # 1 true cointegrating vector: y1 - y2
y = np.zeros((n, 3))
eps = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 3))
for t in range(1, n):
    ec = beta @ y[t-1]                       # long-run disequilibrium
    y[t] = y[t-1] + alpha*ec + eps[t]        # VECM recursion (y3 = pure random walk)
obs = y + rng.normal(0, sig, (n, 3))         # measurement noise contaminates dynamics
j = coint_johansen(obs, det_order=0, k_ar_diff=klag)
trace = j.lr1                                # trace statistics
crit = j.cvt[:, 1]                           # 95% critical values
rank = int(np.sum(trace > crit))
r = np.arange(3); wd = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
ax.bar(r - wd/2, trace, wd, color='#da9100', label='trace stat')
ax.bar(r + wd/2, crit, wd, color='#8fa3b0', label='95% crit')
ax.set_xticks(r); ax.set_xticklabels(['r=0', 'r<=1', 'r<=2'])
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_title(f'Johansen trace -> rank = {rank}  (true rank 1)')
plt.tight_layout()
print(f'sigma={sig:.2f}  lag={klag}  selected rank={rank}  (truth: exactly 1 relation)')
print('trace:', np.round(trace, 1), ' 95% crit:', np.round(crit, 1))

modules.title: 4 · Vector error correction
modules.summary: Combine short-run changes with adjustment toward long-run equilibrium.

stages.title: Vector error correction: research guide
stages.html:
Vector error correction

Combine short-run changes with adjustment toward long-run equilibrium.

The cointegrating vector defines disequilibrium; adjustment coefficients describe which variables respond to that gap.

Workflow. Combine long-run equilibrium errors with short-run changes.

Diagnostic: Inspect adjustment coefficients, cointegrating vectors, and stability. The main failure to avoid is calling every adjustment coefficient a causal response.

stages.title: Vector error correction intuition lab
stages.note: Set the adjustment speed at which y1 error-corrects to the long-run relation, then let statsmodels VECM recover the loading and cointegrating vector — larger speed means the equilibrium error snaps back faster.
stages.template:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.vector_ar.vecm import VECM
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 250; alpha = {{alpha}}; beta = {{beta}}
y1 = np.zeros(n); y2 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    ec = y1[t-1] - beta*y2[t-1]                      # disequilibrium gap
    y2[t] = y2[t-1] + rng.normal(0, 1)               # random-walk driver
    y1[t] = y1[t-1] - alpha*ec + rng.normal(0, 1)    # error-correction pull
data = np.column_stack([y1, y2])
m = VECM(data, k_ar_diff=0, coint_rank=1, deterministic='n').fit()
a_hat = m.alpha.ravel()[0]
bv = m.beta.ravel(); slope_hat = -(bv[1]/bv[0])       # normalized slope
ec_series = y1 - beta*y2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
ax[0].plot(y1, color='#da9100', label='y1'); ax[0].plot(y2, color='#4f8fba', label='y2')
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8); ax[0].set_title('Levels track a common path')
ax[1].plot(ec_series, color='#c0392b'); ax[1].axhline(0, color='#888', lw=0.8)
ax[1].set_title('Equilibrium error (mean-reverts when alpha>0)')
plt.tight_layout()
print(f'true alpha={alpha:.2f}  estimated loading={a_hat:.3f} (|loading| grows with alpha)')
print(f'true beta={beta:.2f}  estimated cointegrating slope={slope_hat:.2f}')

modules.title: 5 · State-space filtering and nowcasting
modules.summary: Estimate latent states and update them as noisy releases arrive.

stages.title: State-space filtering and nowcasting: research guide
stages.html:
State-space filtering and nowcasting

Estimate latent states and update them as noisy releases arrive.

The Kalman filter weighs prior and measurement uncertainty; a real-time nowcast must also respect release dates and data vintages.

Workflow. Update a latent-state estimate by balancing prior and measurement uncertainty.

Diagnostic: Inspect innovation, Kalman gain, and covariance recursion. The main failure to avoid is a state estimate that ignores signal-to-noise information.

stages.title: Kalman filtering intuition lab
stages.note: Run the Kalman recursion on a latent random-walk state — raise the measurement variance to shrink the gain (trust the prior, smooth) or raise the process variance to grow it (chase each release).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200; R = {{R}}; Q = {{Q}}
state = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(Q), n))   # latent random-walk state
obs = state + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(R), n)        # noisy measurements
x_hat = np.zeros(n); x_hat[0] = obs[0]; P = 1.0
gains = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    x_pred = x_hat[t-1]; P_pred = P + Q            # predict step
    K = P_pred / (P_pred + R)                      # Kalman gain
    x_hat[t] = x_pred + K*(obs[t] - x_pred)        # update on innovation
    P = (1 - K)*P_pred                             # covariance recursion
    gains[t] = K
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((x_hat - state)**2))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
ax.plot(obs, '.', color='#c9c6ac', ms=3, label='noisy obs')
ax.plot(state, color='#4f8fba', lw=1.6, label='true state')
ax.plot(x_hat, color='#da9100', lw=1.6, label='Kalman estimate')
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_title(f'steady-state gain={gains[-1]:.2f}   RMSE={rmse:.2f}')
plt.tight_layout()
print(f'R(measure var)={R:.2f}  Q(process var)={Q:.2f}  steady-state gain={gains[-1]:.3f}')
print('High R -> low gain -> trust prior (smooth); high Q -> high gain -> chase the data.')
